lesson.title: Exceptions Have Names: A Map of Python's Built-In Error Types
lesson.summary: Every runtime error in Python is an object of a specific, named type, and recognizing common type names like KeyError or NameError at a glance is one of the fastest ways to read a traceback.
lesson.body:
The overview chapter on errors and exceptions mentioned that a runtime error is an actual object, not just some red text printed to the screen. This chapter goes one level deeper: every exception raised in Python belongs to a specific type, meaning a class, and that type name is exactly what appears at the start of the final line of every traceback you have seen so far, ZeroDivisionError, FileNotFoundError, IndexError, and so on. Knowing the common type names by sight turns a traceback from an intimidating wall of text into a quick diagnosis, because the type name alone tells you roughly what category of problem occurred, before you even read the message after it.

A few of the most common built-in exception types worth recognizing on sight: ZeroDivisionError happens when a number is divided by zero. IndexError happens when a sequence like a list or string is accessed with an index that is out of range for it. KeyError happens when you look up a dictionary key that does not exist in that dictionary. NameError happens when code refers to a variable or function name that has never actually been defined. AttributeError happens when code tries to use a method or attribute that the object in question simply does not have. FileNotFoundError, met in an earlier chapter, happens when open() is given a path that does not exist. Two more, TypeError and ValueError, come up so often and get confused with each other so frequently that they each get their own dedicated chapter right after this one.

You can see the type of an exception directly in code, which is useful once you learn the full mechanics of try and except in a later lesson, since you can inspect exactly what went wrong instead of only reacting to it.

```python
try:
    result = 10 / 0
except Exception as e:
    print(type(e).__name__, ":", e)
```

This prints:

```
ZeroDivisionError : division by zero
```

The except Exception as e line catches the exception and stores the exception object itself in the variable e. type(e) gives back the exact class of that object, ZeroDivisionError in this case, and __name__ turns that class into a plain readable string for printing. Printing e directly, as opposed to type(e), gives just the human-readable message, division by zero, without the type name attached. This is exactly the same information a traceback shows you, type name followed by message, just accessed here as data inside the running program instead of read off the screen after a crash.

The deeper reason this matters is that having a specific type for each kind of problem, rather than one generic "something went wrong" error, is what makes it possible to react differently to different failures, for instance treating a missing file differently from a division by zero, a topic covered fully once you study try and except in depth. For now, treat the type name at the start of a traceback as the single most useful piece of information in it, and build up a working vocabulary of what each common type actually means. TypeError and ValueError, the next two chapters, are the pair most worth getting precisely right.
